extracted.intended_audience: congressional staff, agency officials, administrative law scholars, advocates and regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the causes, effects, and legislative/administrative remedies for 'ossification' of informal (notice-and-comment) rulemaking; aimed at diagnosing why agencies avoid formal rulemaking and how to restore effective, timely, accountable rulemaking. Useful for policymakers and regulators designing reforms or evaluating rulemaking practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive analytical/internal review requirements (prevent ossification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulemaking process became increasingly rigid and cumbersome as presidents, courts and Congress added an assortment of analytical requirements to the simple rulemaking model and as evolving judicial doctrines obliged agencies to take great pains to ensure that the technical bases for rules were capable of withstanding judicial scrutiny under what is now called the 'hard look' doctrine of judicial review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ossification is driven by unnecessary or marginally useful analytical paperwork and internal review burdens. Eliminating marginally useful analytical requirements in statutes and executive orders would likely speed rulemaking, because producing that paperwork is time-consuming and expensive. Congress could enact legislation to reduce or eliminate such requirements; agencies should focus analysis on issues directly relevant to judicial and political arenas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure agencies can meet statutory obligations (timeliness and effectiveness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the pressure of constant opposition from the regulated industries ... statutory deadlines are missed, ambitious policy goals remain unachieved, and the protections envisioned by the authors of the statute gradually erode away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate rulemaking processes by whether agencies can timely promulgate rules to meet statutory goals. If the process prevents agencies from meeting obligations, it is failing: consequences include missed deadlines, unachieved goals, erosion of statutory protections, and taxpayer loss when agencies avoid generic rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve administrative efficiency by favoring generic rulemaking over case-by-case adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative efficiency of promulgating generic rules, rather than making policy on a case-by-case basis, is one of rulemaking’s greatest virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer generic rules where feasible because they are more efficient and predictable. When generic rulemaking becomes too resource-intensive, agencies revert to ad hoc adjudication, losing economies of scale and imposing greater costs on taxpayers and regulated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain incentives to revise rules and to experiment (flexible/temporary rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies have reduced incentives to revise existing rules, even when forced by statute to revisit existing rules, because that would involve a new rulemaking initiative. Experimentation is also riskier in an atmosphere in which any change is likely to involve costly and time-consuming rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A healthy rulemaking regime should lower transaction costs for revising and experimenting with rules (e.g., flexible or temporary rules) so agencies can adapt policies without prohibitive burdens. Evaluate whether procedural requirements discourage updating or piloting approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting adjudication for rulemaking when it evades notice-and-comment
rubrics_metrics.description: The move away from rulemaking to adjudication gives the agency the flexibility to allow policies to evolve through the gradual process of stare decisis ... When agencies resort to articulating rules in adjudications as a vehicle for avoiding informal rulemaking, however, regulatees are no longer put on notice of the standards of conduct that the agency is applying to them and both regulatee and beneficiary groups are deprived of the opportunity that informal rulemaking provides to influence the agency’s thinking on the rule through the comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy developed via adjudication may escape public notice and comment and reduce regulatory legitimacy. Evaluate whether agencies are using adjudication to avoid broad rulemaking and whether affected parties are being denied notice and the opportunity to comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit non-rule rulemaking (guidance documents, policy statements, manuals, interim final rules) as substitutes for formal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Although informal guidance documents and technical manuals are a necessary part of a complex administrative regime, agencies typically issue them without the benefit of public comments. Adopting these less formal devices as a way to avoid burdensome and intrusive rulemaking requirements therefore renders regulatory agencies much less accountable to the public and paves the way to arbitrary decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish necessary guidance from de facto rules that should undergo notice-and-comment. Ensure accountability and public participation when documents have binding effects; scrutinize the use of interim final rules and interpretative rules to circumvent APA procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address stakeholder delay tactics and 'blood sport' rulemaking strategies
rubrics_metrics.description: My 2012 article on 'blood sport' rulemaking highlights many of the tactics that stakeholders now use for slowing down or influencing the outcome of high-stakes rulemaking proceedings, many of which are employed outside the APA’s notice-and-comment process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how outside actors (regulated industries, think tanks, trade associations, lobbyists) deploy procedural and extra-procedural tactics to slow or shape rulemakings. Reforms should aim to reduce opportunities for crippling delay while preserving meaningful participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase systemic congressional oversight of the rulemaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thing that Congress can do to fix the broken informal rulemaking model is to step up its oversight of the rulemaking process and of the roles that agency staffs, desk officers in the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), lobbyists for regulatees and beneficiary groups, think tanks, trade associations, and ordinary citizens play in that process. Congressional oversight of rulemaking should be systemic and not limited to inquiries into particular rulemaking exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oversight should be ongoing and comprehensive, examining structural incentives, OIRA interactions, and the influence of external actors rather than just ad hoc reviews of individual rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amend statutes that are interpreted to require more formal procedures than section 553
rubrics_metrics.description: Some agencies like OSHA believe that their statutes mandate a more formal rulemaking process than the notice-and-comment process envisioned by section 553. Congress could amend those statutes to make its intent clear that formal hearings and other formal procedures are not necessary in particular contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where statutory language is causing unnecessary procedural burdens, Congress can clarify intent to allow appropriate levels of formality. Review statutory texts that agencies construe as requiring more onerous procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit OIRA's substantive intervention and increase transparency of OIRA review
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary objection to OIRA review of rulemaking is that OIRA’s input often goes beyond comments on the agency’s analysis to demands that the agency change the substance of the rules. Unidentified White House officials can use the OIRA review process to advance policies that run counter to the agencies’ statutes. ... Abuse of the OIRA review process can be limited and its accountability enhanced by increasing its transparency. OIRA review is not governed by the Administrative Procedure Act, and the transparency of that review process has waxed and waned over the years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the OIRA review process for transparency, adherence to stated 'rules of engagement,' and whether it stays within a reviewer's role. Consider statutory or policy changes to make OIRA interactions public and constrained to analytic comments rather than substantive rule rewriting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce White House de facto control over agency decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies are understandably reluctant to cede decisionmaking authority to OIRA, and Congress should be equally concerned about the White House’s de facto exercise of unconstrained power over the agencies’ implementation of congressional goals. Much of what motivates the agencies to attempt to circumvent the rulemaking process is the prospect dealing with the acrimonious and time-consuming process of OIRA review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms should seek to limit the White House's capacity to substitute its policy preferences for those set by Congress and the agencies' statutory mandates, for example by cutting back White House oversight or increasing formal constraints and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider changes to judicial review scope for informal rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress might think about enacting legislation designed to signal to the courts its intention that they reduce the intensity of judicial review of informal rulemaking. It could, for example, amend the APA to change the scope of review for informal rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a politically and legally fraught option (hard to specify less intensive review than 'arbitrary and capricious'), but lawmakers and scholars should consider whether the intensity of judicial review is creating perverse incentives that cause agencies to avoid rulemaking; courts may also adjust doctrines with scholarly input.
